title: Writing a Simple Business Plan
summary: Build a clear one-page business plan, test your idea with a simple survey, estimate start-up costs and funding, and make a six-month cash forecast and a two-minute pitch.
audience: Students, young entrepreneurs and small business owners who want to plan a new venture

lessons.title: The one-page plan: problem, customers and offer

body.p: A business plan is a short written answer to one question: how will this idea earn enough money to survive? A plan does not need to be long. For a small business a single page is a strong start, because it forces you to be clear. The plan also helps when you ask a bank, a family member or a competition panel for support.

list: Problem: what difficulty do people have that you can solve?
Customers: who exactly has this problem and will pay to fix it?
Offer: what do you sell, and why is it better or different?
Competitors: who else solves this problem today, including informal sellers?
Marketing: how will customers hear about you and decide to buy?
Operations: how do you make or deliver the product each day?
Team: who does what, and what skills do they bring?
Money: what will it cost, what will you charge, and when will cash arrive?

body.p: Start with the problem and customers, because everything else depends on them. A weak example: 'I will sell snacks.' It does not say who needs them or why. A stronger version: 'Students at the college gate have 20 minutes between lectures and cannot find a hot, filling snack that costs less than a full meal. I will sell fresh wraps from a stand opposite the main gate at lunchtime.' Now there is a problem, a customer, a place and a time.

A customer description should be specific enough to picture. Compare 'everyone' with 'students aged 17 to 24 who live within ten minutes of the college and spend on lunch every day'. The second can be reached with a flyer, a social media group or a stand. The first cannot be reached efficiently by any small business.

steps: Write one sentence that starts: 'People who ... have trouble with ...'
Write who they are, where they are and how many you might reach.
Write what you will sell and one reason they will pick you instead of what they use now.
Say what they will pay and how often they will buy.
Read it aloud to someone who is not in the business. If they cannot repeat it back, simplify.

body.tip: Write the plan in plain words and short sentences. A good test is whether a friend who has never heard of your idea can understand it in under two minutes.

lessons.title: Market research with a simple survey

body.p: Market research means finding out what real people want before you spend money. You do not need an expensive study. Two cheap methods work well: talking to people one to one, and a short survey of potential customers. Use both, because conversation tells you why and numbers tell you how many.

A good survey is short, no more than six or seven questions, and easy to answer on a phone or on paper. Ask about behaviour rather than opinion where you can. Asking 'Would you buy a hot wrap?' invites a polite yes. Asking 'What did you buy for lunch yesterday, and how much did you spend?' tells you what people truly do.

list: Who are you? (age group, student or worker, area) so you can tell which customers answer which way.
What do you do now? (where do you buy this today, how often, how much do you spend)
What is wrong with it? (price, quality, distance, waiting time)
Would you try mine at this price? (yes, maybe, no)
What would make you come back?

body.p: Be careful about bias. If you ask only your friends and family, they may say what you want to hear. Try to ask people who do not know you, in the place where your customers actually are. Offer the choices in a neutral way and do not hint at the answer you hope for.

Worked example. You ask 50 students and 31 say yes to trying your wrap at the planned price. The share is 31 / 50 = 62%. Suppose about 1,200 students pass your stand during lunch. Then 1,200 x 31 / 50 = 744 students say they would try it. People often say yes and then do not buy, so be cautious. If you assume only half follow through, that is 744 / 2 = 372 students. This is a planning estimate and not a promise, and it is better to be cautious. The 50 people you asked should look like the 1,200 you are counting, otherwise the number is not reliable.

body.tip: Write down how many you asked and how you picked them. A small sample, like 50, gives a rough idea only. If the answers are close to even, such as 26 yes and 24 no, do not treat the result as a clear signal. Ask more people or test with a small trial sale.

body.p: Every business has competitors, even if nobody else sells exactly the same thing. A competitor is anything your customer might use instead of you, including a roadside seller, a shop, a cheaper product, or doing the job themselves. List the three or four main ones and note their price, quality, location and what customers say about them. A visit or a short chat with their customers tells you more than guessing.

Worked example. Three nearby sellers charge 8, 10 and 12 for a similar wrap. The average is (8 + 10 + 12) / 3 = 10. You plan to charge 9. Being 1 below the average is only a good idea if your costs allow it. Cheaper is not the only way to win. You can offer faster service, a clean stand, bigger portions, or a loyalty card.

Marketing is how people find out about you, trust you and buy. Choose methods that reach your specific customers cheaply: word of mouth, a sign at the right place, a social media group or messaging group, flyers, and free samples. Track what works by asking each new customer how they heard about you.

Measure the cost of winning customers. If you spend 150 on flyers and free samples in a month and gain 30 new regular customers, the cost per new customer is 150 / 30 = 5. If a regular customer is likely to give you more profit than that over the next few months, the marketing is worth repeating. If not, change the method.

list: Operations: write the steps of a normal day, from buying stock to serving the customer to cleaning up. Note equipment, suppliers, place, opening hours and where things can go wrong.
Suppliers: have a second supplier for key items, so you can still work if the first one fails.
Team: list who does each task, what they are good at, and any gaps. Gaps can be filled by training, a partner, a part-time helper, or an adviser.
Rules and licences: some businesses need permits, safety checks or registration. These differ by country and town, so ask your local business office rather than assuming.

body.tip: If you work alone, be honest in the team section about what you are weaker at, such as keeping records or selling, and say how you will get help. Funders respect honesty more than a claim that you can do everything.

body.p: Start-up costs are the one-time amounts you must spend before the business can earn its first sale. Missing items from this list is the commonest planning mistake, so go through each part of your plan and ask: what do I need to buy or pay for to make this work? Include a cash cushion, sometimes called working capital, to cover the first weeks when costs are high and sales are still growing.

body.code:
Equipment (oven, tables, scales)                          1,800
First stock of ingredients                                  700
Registration, permits and deposits (check local fees)       650
Marketing launch (signs, flyers)                            200
Cash cushion for the first weeks                            650
TOTAL START-UP COSTS                                      4,000

body.p: Add the items: 1,800 + 700 + 650 + 200 + 650 = 4,000. Do not copy these numbers. They are a worked example, and your prices and fees will be different. Get at least two quotes for big items, and check the real fee for any permit locally.

list: Own savings: no one to repay, but you risk your own money.
Family and friends: cheaper and flexible, but write down the amount and the repayment plan so relationships stay healthy.
Loans from banks, microfinance or savings groups: you must repay with interest or fees, so only borrow what your cash forecast shows you can repay.
Grants and business competitions: you do not repay, but they take time and are competitive, so never depend on one that you have not won.
Supplier credit: the supplier lets you pay later, which helps your cash, but you still owe the money.
Customer pre-orders or deposits: customers pay before you deliver.

body.p: Worked example of a funding plan for the 4,000 need: own savings 1,500, loan from family 1,000, small grant or competition prize 800, supplier credit (pay later) 700. Total = 4,000, which matches the start-up costs. As shares of the total: own savings 37.5%, loan from family 25.0%, small grant or competition prize 20.0%, supplier credit (pay later) 17.5%. Notice that a grant and supplier credit are uncertain, so a safer plan keeps a reserve in case one falls through.

body.tip: Before you borrow, ask: what is the total amount I must repay, how often, and what happens if a month is slow? If you cannot answer, do not sign. Rules on lending differ in each country, so read any agreement carefully and ask someone you trust to read it too.

body.p: A cash forecast shows, month by month, the money you expect to receive and to pay, and the cash left at the end of each month. It answers the question that kills many businesses: will I have enough cash to pay my bills on time? A business can be profitable on paper and still run out of cash if customers pay late or if big payments fall in the same month.

Worked example. The wrap business sells at 9 each. The ingredients for each wrap cost 5. Fixed costs each month are rent 300, wages 400 and marketing 100, so 800 in total. A loan repayment of 150 starts in month 4. It begins with 500 cash after start-up. Expected sales are 200, 240, 290, 340, 380, 420 wraps in months 1 to 6, and customers pay cash on the spot.

steps: Cash in for the month = units x price. Month 1: 200 x 9 = 1,800.
Ingredients = units x cost per unit. Month 1: 200 x 5 = 1,000.
Total cash out = ingredients + fixed costs + loan repayment. Month 1: 1,000 + 800 + 0 = 1,800.
Net cash = cash in - cash out. Month 1: 1,800 - 1,800 = 0.
Closing cash = opening cash + net cash. Month 1: 500 + 0 = 500. This closing figure is the next month's opening cash.
Month 4 includes the loan repayment: cash out = 1,700 + 800 + 150 = 2,650, so net cash = 3,060 - 2,650 = 410.

body.p: Break-even is where sales just cover the fixed costs. Each wrap leaves 9 - 5 = 4 after ingredients. Break-even units = 800 / 4 = 200 wraps a month, which month 1 just reaches. By month 6, cash is 2,730.

Always test a worse case. If sales are 20% lower, the units become 160, 192, 232, 272, 304, 336. Month 1 cash in is 1,440 and cash out is 1,600, giving net cash of -160. The lowest closing cash in that case is 308 in month 2, and the business stays above zero. If the lowest figure had been negative, you would need more start-up cash or lower costs.

body.tip: Keep the forecast in a simple spreadsheet or on paper with the same rows each month. Update it with real numbers every month and write down the difference. Your forecast improves with practice.

lessons.title: Risks, back-up plans and the two-minute pitch

body.p: Every plan has risks, things that might go wrong. Listing them is a sign of good planning, not weakness. For each risk, estimate how likely it is and how serious it would be, then decide what you will do about it. One simple method scores each from 1 (low) to 3 (high) and multiplies them.

body.code:
Risk                        Likelihood  Impact  Score
Main oven breaks                 2        3       6
A rival opens nearby             3        2       6
Ingredient prices rise           3        3       9
Owner falls ill                  1        3       3

body.p: Score = likelihood x impact. Scores here are Main oven breaks 6, A rival opens nearby 6, Ingredient prices rise 9, Owner falls ill 3. The highest is ingredient prices rising at 9, so it needs a plan first: for example keep a second supplier, buy larger amounts when prices are low, or change the menu or the price. Note that a low-likelihood risk can still matter. The owner falling ill has a score of only 3 but would stop the whole business, so a back-up person who knows the routine is worthwhile.

list: Back-up for equipment: know a repair person and keep a small repair fund.
Back-up for sales: a second product or a second sales channel, such as delivery or orders by message.
Back-up for cash: a reserve that covers at least a few weeks of fixed costs, and a list of costs you can cut quickly.
Back-up for people: write the daily routine so someone else can follow it.

body.p: A pitch is a short talk that explains the plan and asks for something, such as a loan, a place in a programme or support. Speaking at a comfortable pace of about 130 words per minute, two minutes is about 130 x 2 = 260 words, so write about that many and practise aloud with a timer. Split the 120 seconds like this.

list: Problem: 20 seconds
Solution and offer: 25 seconds
Customers and competitors: 20 seconds
Money: 35 seconds
The ask and next step: 20 seconds

body.p: In the money part, say how much you need, what it pays for, and when and how you will repay or reach break-even. In the final part, say exactly what you are asking for. Use one or two real numbers from your survey and your forecast, because they make you believable. Practise in front of a friend and ask what they remember.

body.tip: Do not read from a page. Write five key words, one for each part, and talk. If you lose your place, look at your key words, take a breath and carry on.

quiz.q: Which sentence is the clearest description of customers for a business plan?
options: Everyone who likes good food
People with money
Students aged 17 to 24 who live near the college and buy lunch every day
Anybody who walks past

quiz.q: What is the main reason to include a back-up plan in a business plan?
options: To show what you will do if a likely or serious risk happens
To prove that nothing can go wrong
To make the plan longer
To avoid doing a cash forecast

quiz.q: In a survey, 45 of 60 people say they would try your product. What percentage is that?
You survey only your close friends about your new business idea. What is the main problem?
options: Friends never buy anything
They may say what you want to hear, so the result can be biased
The survey will cost too much
Surveys must have at least 1,000 people

quiz.q: There are 800 households in an area. In a survey 40% said they would buy. Assume only half of them really buy. How many households is that?
Four competitors charge 14, 16, 18 and 20. What is the average price?
You spend 240 on marketing and win 48 new customers. What is the cost per new customer?
Start-up costs are: 2500, 900, 1200, 600, 300. What is the total?
A business needs 6,500 to start. The owner has 2,000 and expects a loan of 3,000. How much more funding is needed?
What is working capital in a start-up budget?
options: Cash kept to pay running costs while sales are still growing
The total value of the equipment
The money the owner takes as salary
The profit made in the first year

quiz.q: A product sells for 12 and costs 7 to make. Fixed costs are 1,500 a month. How many units must be sold per month to break even?
A month starts with 400 cash. Cash in is 2,500 and cash out is 2,850. What is the closing cash?
A forecast starts with cash of 300. Net cash flows for months 1 to 4 are -250, -150, +90 and +200. In which month does closing cash first go below zero?
options: Month 1
Month 4
Month 2
It never goes below zero

quiz.q: A bakery shows a profit on paper but cannot pay its supplier on time. What is the most likely cause?
options: Customers pay late, or cash was spent on stock and equipment, so cash is short even though profit exists
Profit and cash are always the same figure
Suppliers never want to be paid
Profit means there is no need for a cash forecast

quiz.q: A risk has likelihood 3 and impact 3. Another has likelihood 1 and impact 3. Which statement is correct?
options: The scores are 6 and 4; ignore the second
Both are the same score
The second is higher because its impact is the same
The scores are 9 and 3; deal with the first one first, but still have a back-up for the second

quiz.q: You speak at 130 words per minute. About how many words fit a two-minute pitch?
